what_it_does: Microcontrollers are tiny, low-power chips (think the processor inside a thermostat or a hearing aid) with very little memory and compute — yet researchers want to run small AI networks on them. One strategy is to avoid redoing computations when the same or similar input values appear repeatedly; prior approaches defined 'reuse' narrowly, so they missed many opportunities. This paper reframes the problem: rearranging the rows and columns of the data tables that the AI network processes exposes far more opportunities to reuse earlier results, and different rearrangements reveal different savings. The authors build two lightweight mathematical models — one predicting how much accuracy the network loses from approximations introduced by reuse, the other predicting how fast the resulting computation will run on the specific microcontroller — and use these models to search automatically for the best rearrangement strategy for a given network and chip.
